name: Ishmael
role: Narrator; a schoolmaster turned common sailor
desc:
A former schoolmaster and merchant sailor who signs on as an ordinary whaleman. He gives little settled description of his own appearance; the book makes his habits of attention far more distinctive.

Restless, curious, humorous and sometimes melancholy, he goes to sea to escape a stifling life ashore. He is drawn to unfamiliar people, religious practices and bodies of knowledge. He narrates with a mixture of personal experience, speculation and imaginative reconstruction, so the scope of his voice often exceeds what a single sailor could witness.
why: He is the book's real experiment: a man who survives by being porous, by being willing to sleep with a cannibal, squeeze spermaceti with strangers, and take every subject seriously. Ahab has one meaning; Ishmael has all of them.

name: Queequeg
role: Harpooneer of Starbuck's boat; prince of Kokovoko
desc:
A powerful harpooneer from the island of Kokovoko, with an extensively tattooed face and body and a mostly shaved head. His harpoon, small idol and unfamiliar customs initially alarm Ishmael. He serves in Starbuck's boat.

Calm, dignified, generous and highly competent, he expresses friendship through practical actions. He is comfortable with habits that Ishmael finds strange and shows little need to defend them. Ishmael's changing response to him helps the reader distinguish outward unfamiliarity from character.
why: The book's moral centre without ever making a speech. His tenderness is practical — he saves the bumpkin who mocked him, dives for Tashtego — and it is his coffin that carries Ishmael out. Melville makes the “savage” the one civilized man aboard.

name: Captain Ahab
desc:
The Pequod's aging captain, tall and powerfully built, with gray hair and a pale, scar-like mark running down his face and neck. One leg has been replaced by a prosthesis made from whale bone after an encounter with Moby Dick.

Commanding, solitary and intensely purposeful, he speaks in a heightened, theatrical style. Long experience gives him real authority at sea. His anger at the white whale is deeply personal, and his ability to turn that anger into a shared purpose shapes life aboard the ship.
why: What fascinates me is that he is right about a great deal. His speeches on the pasteboard mask, on the doubloon, on the sea's sweetness in The Symphony, are the truest things anyone says. He is the terrible proof that clarity is not the same as wisdom.

name: Starbuck
desc:
The chief mate, a Nantucket Quaker with a lean, weathered appearance. He has a wife and young son ashore. As first mate he commands one of the hunting boats, with Queequeg as his harpooneer.

Serious, conscientious and deeply religious, he treats courage as compatible with a sensible fear of danger. He sees whaling as work undertaken for a livelihood, rather than a private crusade. His restrained manner and concern for duty distinguish him from Ahab and from the other mates.
why: He is the reader's stand-in for ordinary decency and I find him almost unbearably sad. He is the man who knows and cannot act; his goodness has no traction against a will like Ahab's, which is maybe the book's harshest observation about goodness.

name: Stubb
desc:
The second mate, from Cape Cod, almost inseparable from his pipe. He commands the boat in which Tashtego serves as harpooneer. His relaxed bearing is as distinctive as his constant smoking.

Easygoing, joking and highly practiced, he meets danger as though it were familiar routine. His good humor can shade into indifference to other people's discomfort. He often makes a joke where Starbuck would raise a moral concern or Flask would look for a fight.
why: His philosophy — “I know not all that may be coming, but be it what it will, I'll go to it laughing” — is one of the book's genuine alternatives to Ahab, and Melville lets you feel both its charm and its shallowness. He is also cruel to Fleece and to Pip in ways the joking doesn't cover.

name: Flask
desc:
The third mate, a short, stout, ruddy young man from Martha's Vineyard. His compact build earns him the nickname King-Post. The much taller Daggoo is his harpooneer.

Pugnacious, energetic and impatient, he treats whales chiefly as creatures to be killed and processed. He has little of Starbuck's reverence or Stubb's reflective joking. His eagerness for action and his physical contrast with Daggoo make their boat easy to recognize.
why: He is what a whaler is without any inner life at all — and Melville is kind enough to give him one small moment on the last day, wishing his mother had drawn his part-pay.

name: Tashtego
role: Harpooneer of Stubb's boat; Gay Head Wampanoag
desc:
An Indigenous harpooneer from Gay Head on Martha's Vineyard, with a lean, agile build, long dark hair, high cheekbones and dark eyes. He serves in Stubb's boat.

Skillful and physically assured, he brings the precision of a hunter to the whaling work. Ishmael repeatedly connects him with an inherited tradition of hunting. Remember his pairing with Stubb when the narrative moves quickly between the three mates' boats.
why: His last act is the book's final image: a hand still hammering as the ship goes down, dragging a piece of heaven with it.

name: Daggoo
role: Harpooneer of Flask's boat; from Africa
desc:
An African harpooneer, six feet five inches tall, with a powerful build and large gold hoops in his ears. His commanding physical presence contrasts sharply with the small stature of Flask, the mate whose boat he serves.

Experienced, composed and confident in his strength, he carries himself with dignity. Ishmael's descriptions often make him appear more imposing than the officer above him. The contrast helps reveal the difference between a person's rank and the authority of their presence.
why: Melville gives him less interiority than the other two harpooneers, which I notice and regret; but the image of a white mate standing on a Black man's shoulders to hunt is not accidental.

name: Fedallah
desc:
A tall, dark-complexioned Parsee associated closely with Ahab. He wears dark clothing, and his white hair is braided and wound around his head like a turban. One conspicuous tooth adds to Ishmael's unsettling portrait.

Reserved and mysterious, he stands apart from the ordinary social life of the crew. Other sailors attach superstitious explanations to his influence. His speech and his relationship with Ahab draw on prophecy and religious imagery rather than the mates' practical language of work.
why: He is the one character I can't settle: a genuine Mephistopheles, or an ordinary Persian sailor onto whom the crew projects their dread? The book lets him be both, and his death — lashed to the whale by the tangled lines, going before Ahab — is the coldest thing in it.

name: Pip
role: Ship-keeper and cabin boy; from Alabama
desc:
A small Black boy from Connecticut who plays the tambourine aboard the Pequod. His youth and slight stature set him apart from the experienced sailors and harpooneers.

Lively, sensitive and vulnerable, he brings music and play into the ship's harsh working world. His position is especially insecure when he is expected to take on dangerous boat work. Attend to the way other men respond to him: those responses reveal much about the ship's hierarchy and its capacity for care.
why: Pip is the book's second answer to what the ocean does to a mind — Ahab's is rage, Pip's is a kind of holy idiocy that sees “God's foot upon the treadle of the loom.” The scenes where Ahab holds his hand are the only tenderness Ahab is allowed.

name: Bulkington
desc:
A sailor first noticed at the Spouter-Inn, about six feet tall, with broad shoulders, a powerful chest and a deeply sunburned face. Ishmael hears a Southern accent in his voice. His shipmates clearly like him.

Quiet and reserved amid their noisy celebration, he seems drawn back toward the sea even after a long voyage. His brief presence gives Ishmael a way to think about independence and the difficulty of remaining safely ashore.
why: Melville apparently meant him for a larger part and then didn't write it. What remains is one of the book's purest passages about why anyone goes to sea, and a ghost of the novel that wasn't.

name: Dough-Boy
desc:
The Pequod's steward, a pale young man whose round, soft-looking face gives him his nickname. He serves meals in the cabin and attends to the officers and harpooneers at table.

Nervous and easily intimidated, he is especially uneasy around the forceful harpooneers. His flinching, hurried manner provides a domestic contrast to their physical confidence. Through his work, the reader sees how rank and temperament shape even ordinary meals aboard ship.
why: Comic, but a real piece of the ship's economy of fear — the cabin table is a small monarchy and Dough-Boy is its trembling clerk.

name: Fleece
desc:
The ship's very elderly Black cook, stiff in his joints and burdened by long years of work. He is responsible for feeding the men and is sometimes summoned from sleep to satisfy an officer's wishes.

Plainspoken, weary and capable of dry humor, he has little patience for needless demands. His exchanges with Stubb expose the imbalance between an officer's amusement and a servant's labor. His impromptu speech to the sharks turns that comic situation into a reflection on appetite and self-control.
why: The scene is played for laughs and lands, but reread it: Fleece's sermon is better theology than Father Mapple's, and Stubb's treatment of him is one of the places the book's racial cruelty is not just observed but performed.

name: Perth
desc:
The Pequod's elderly blacksmith, an accomplished metalworker with a painful history ashore. The narrative describes his damaged circumstances and enduring skill more fully than his appearance.

Patient, subdued and hardworking, he keeps his forge busy with repairs and special commissions. Grief and the consequences of drinking lie behind his decision to live at sea. His quiet craftsmanship provides a contrast to the elevated language and fierce purposes of the captain who employs it.
why: His chapter is about how the sea receives the wrecked — “Death seems the only desirable sequel for a career like this” — and it sits deliberately before The Forge.

name: The Carpenter
desc:
An unnamed craftsman responsible for the ship's woodwork, fittings and many improvised repairs. His dexterous hands and practical habits are more distinctive than his physical appearance.

Matter-of-fact, adaptable and emotionally detached, he treats unusual requests as jobs requiring a solution. His usefulness extends well beyond carpentry. His literal, workmanlike responses can sit oddly beside Ahab's philosophical and dramatic speech.
why: Ahab talks to him as to a machine, and the carpenter's blank competence is a mirror Ahab keeps peering into. Also: he builds the thing that saves Ishmael.

name: The Manxman
role: Old sailor from the Isle of Man
desc:
An old, gray-haired sailor from the Isle of Man, with a grave, almost funereal presence. He belongs to the experienced hands whose sea knowledge includes inherited beliefs and superstitions.

Watchful and solemn, he interprets appearances, sounds and objects as omens. Other sailors take his judgments seriously. His confidence in signs gives the reader a different kind of knowledge from Ishmael's investigations or the officers' seamanship.
why: Every ship has one; Melville uses him like a chorus.

name: Father Mapple
desc:
An elderly but vigorous preacher in New Bedford, formerly a sailor and harpooneer. His weathered face and physically agile ascent of the rope ladder to his ship-shaped pulpit connect his ministry with his earlier life at sea.

Warm in presence and forceful in speech, he preaches through maritime images his listeners understand. He emphasizes duty, obedience to God and the courage to tell an unwelcome truth. His sermon establishes moral questions that remain active throughout the voyage.
why: The sermon is the book's ethical thesis and Ahab is the book's refutation of it, or the reverse; I still can't decide which, which is why it's a great sermon.

name: Captain Peleg & Captain Bildad
desc:
Two retired whaling captains and part owners of the Pequod who hire and provision its crew. Peleg is blustering and profane; Bildad is an austere older Quaker, associated with sober dress and his Bible.

Peleg negotiates through noise, experience and rough generosity. Bildad speaks the language of piety while watching costs closely. Their contrasting habits help explain the commercial world behind the voyage: sailors' wages, religious professions and profits are all being considered together.
why: Bildad's parting — “Don't stave the boats needlessly, ye harpooneers” — is a whole moral universe in a sentence.

name: Elijah
role: A prophet on the Nantucket wharf
desc:
A ragged stranger with a pockmarked face, encountered near the Pequod before it sails. His appearance and cryptic manner make him hard for Ishmael to place socially.

He asks unsettling questions about Ahab and the men's decision to join the ship. His warnings come as hints rather than clear explanations. His biblical name and prophetic style invite attention, while leaving Ishmael unsure how seriously to take him.
why: Named for the prophet who denounced King Ahab; ignored, as prophets are.

name: Peter Coffin & Mrs. Hussey
desc:
Peter Coffin keeps the Spouter-Inn in New Bedford; Mrs. Hussey runs the Try Pots in Nantucket. They belong to separate inns and different stages of Ishmael and Queequeg's journey toward the Pequod.

Coffin has a dry, mischievous humor and enjoys leaving Ishmael uncertain about his prospective bedfellow. Mrs. Hussey is brisk and practical, concerned with meals, house rules and the safety of her guests. Their everyday authority contrasts with the grand language of the voyage.
why: The comedy of the shore chapters is real comedy, and the name Coffin is the first of the book's coffins.

name: Aunt Charity
desc:
Captain Bildad's sister, an energetic woman who helps prepare the Pequod for sea. She appears with useful provisions and small necessities rather than with a detailed description of her looks.

Generous, attentive and practically minded, she notices needs that are easily missed in the business of outfitting a ship. Her kindness is expressed through supplies, comforts and care for the sailors. She gives a human dimension to the commercial arrangements made by her brother and Peleg.
why: A small kindness set against everything the voyage becomes.

name: Captain Boomer
desc:
The English captain of the Samuel Enderby, recognizable by the ivory prosthetic arm that replaced an arm lost to Moby Dick. He is sociable and given to joking, including with the surgeon who treated him.

His experience resembles Ahab's in one important respect, but he responds to the injury differently. He regards the white whale as a danger to avoid rather than an enemy demanding revenge. That difference helps clarify how personal Ahab's interpretation of the whale is.
why: The book's control experiment: a man with Ahab's wound and none of Ahab's disease.

name: Gabriel
desc:
A small, short, youngish sailor aboard the Jeroboam, with a freckled face, abundant yellow hair and an unusual long coat. He presents himself as a religious prophet and takes his name from the archangel.

Fiercely convinced of his own visions, he gains influence by frightening the crew. His claims draw on his Shaker background and on apocalyptic imagery. His warnings about the white whale show how fear and religious certainty can become a form of authority at sea.
why: Ahab's madness seen in a lesser, uglier register — and Gabriel is, unlike Ahab, right about what happens next.

name: Captain Gardiner
desc:
The Nantucket captain of the Rachel, encountered in a state of visible distress while searching for a missing boat that includes his young son. His pallor and urgent appeals make his anxiety immediately apparent.

A father as well as a working captain, he places the search for people above the pursuit of whales. His concern is specific and personal. His request for help makes the reader consider the obligations one ship and one captain have toward another.
why: The Rachel, “weeping for her children,” is what finds Ishmael at the end. I think this is the book's one act of grace and it comes from a man Ahab turned away.

name: Steelkilt & Radney
desc:
Two men from the story of the Town-Ho. Steelkilt is a tall, powerful Great Lakes sailor with a flowing golden beard; Radney is the ship's mate, described as physically unattractive, tough and stubborn.

Steelkilt is proud, capable and unwilling to accept humiliation. Radney is overbearing and resentful of the sailor's commanding presence. Their conflict turns on dignity and rank: one man possesses formal power, while the other refuses to let that power define his worth.
why: A whole revenge novel embedded in the whale novel, and the first time we see Moby Dick act as if he were justice.

name: Derick de Deer
desc:
The German captain of the Jungfrau, a whaling ship from Bremen. He approaches the Pequod with containers for oil because his own ship has run short. The episode emphasizes his equipment and activity more than a detailed physical portrait.

Eager and competitive, he is anxious to turn his voyage into a success. Ishmael presents his efforts with a strong comic edge. His encounter offers another view of whaling as an international business in which experience, judgment and luck matter as much as ambition.
why: Melville's comedy of nations; also the chapter with the book's cruelest, most tender whale-death.

name: Moby Dick
desc:
An exceptionally large sperm whale, distinguished by a white forehead and hump, a deeply wrinkled brow and a distorted lower jaw. Old harpoons lodged in his body suggest earlier encounters with hunters. He is a particular whale, not the name of the species.

Sailors circulate stories about his strength, cunning and apparent ability to escape pursuit. Those reports combine observed danger with rumor. Different people give him different meanings, so it helps to distinguish the animal's physical presence from what Ahab and others believe he represents.
why: Melville is careful never to tell you what the whale means and equally careful to let every character tell you. The whiteness chapter is the key: what terrifies is not malice but the possibility of no meaning at all. And then, in the chase, the whale is just an animal, magnificent and pursued.
